Last term I had a trick for maths homework. First I'd sharpen all my pencils. Then I'd tidy my desk, even the drawer. Then I'd ask Mummy for water. Then I'd do my Hindi homework twice. By then it was dinner. Every day the maths got scarier, because I hadn't looked at it, and every day I tidied more.
My brother Harish noticed. "Your desk is cleaner than a hospital," he said. "And your maths book still has the price sticker on it." One evening he sat next to me and said, "Just do the first question. Only that." I got it wrong, then right. It wasn't as bad as the scary feeling said. I'm Parul, and I still sharpen my pencils, but now I do question one first.

qa.q: What did Harish say Parul's maths book still had on it?
qa.a: The price sticker.

qa.q: Why did tidying and fetching water feel better to Parul than opening the maths book?
qa.a: Not knowing how to do the maths felt uncomfortable, and each small escape gave instant relief, even though the fear kept growing.

qa.q: What small step broke the pattern for Parul?
qa.a: Harish sitting beside Parul and saying 'Just do the first question', which made starting feel possible. 🙂

qa.q: How did Harish see Parul's spotless desk?
qa.a: He saw through it, noticing the tidy desk and the untouched maths book, and guessed Parul was avoiding the hard part.

grounding: A child looks back on avoiding maths homework by tidying and fetching water, until a brother helps with just the first question.

Tuition teacher's note, Wednesday
Karthik, age 9, has a pattern with his science worksheets. As soon as I hand one out, he asks to fill his water bottle. Then he sharpens his pencil. Then he rearranges his pencil box by colour. Twenty minutes pass and the sheet is blank.
I think the science questions make him feel he doesn't know enough, and each little errand gives him a break from that feeling. But the longer he waits, the bigger the sheet seems.
Today I sat beside him and covered all but the first question with a card. "Just this one," I said. He answered it in two minutes. Then the next. He finished half the sheet and grinned.
Next step: I'll tell his mother about the card trick for home.
Sabina

qa.q: What did Sabina cover the worksheet with?
qa.a: A card.

qa.q: Why does Karthik keep going on little errands when the science worksheet arrives?
qa.a: The questions make him feel he doesn't know enough, and each errand gives him a short break from that uncomfortable feeling.

qa.q: Which choice of Sabina's helped, and why?
qa.a: Covering all but the first question, so the task looked small enough to start, and each answer built his confidence.

qa.q: What might Karthik's mother notice once the card trick is used at home?
qa.a: Probably that he starts homework sooner and fusses less, since one question at a time feels manageable.

grounding: A tuition teacher notes a boy who escapes hard science worksheets through small errands, and helps him start with one question.

Diary, Monday
I have a Sanskrit translation due on Friday and I haven't even opened the chapter. It's the hardest thing we do. Instead, today I watered all the plants, sorted my stickers, cleaned my shoes and asked Amma for water three times. Amma said, "Are you a camel?"
Every time I think of the chapter, my tummy goes tight. When I do something else, it goes loose again. So I keep doing something else. But now it's Monday night, and the chapter is bigger in my head than it was on Saturday.
Tanvir from my class said he does five minutes with a timer. Just five. Tomorrow I'll try it right after milk. Five minutes can't kill me.
Sudha

qa.a: "Are you a camel?"

qa.q: Why does Sudha keep 'doing something else' instead of the translation?
qa.a: Sudha feels anxious about the hard chapter, and the tummy goes tight at the thought of it; other jobs bring quick relief, so escaping wins for now.

qa.q: What small step does Sudha plan, and why might it work?
qa.a: Five minutes with a timer right after milk, which makes starting small enough to face so the chapter stops growing.

qa.q: What might Amma be thinking as the requests for water keep coming?
qa.a: Amma may sense Sudha is avoiding something, and the camel joke hints that she has noticed.

grounding: A child avoids a hard translation by doing chores and asking for water, notices the task growing bigger, and plans a five-minute start.

In the village near Moga, the English grammar exercise sat inside Lokesh's school bag all evening. Tenses. The one subject where every sentence looked like a trap.

First he gave the calves fresh water. Then he wiped his little wooden shelf until it shone. Then he swept the courtyard, which nobody had asked him to do. "Bebe, can I have water?" he called, twice.

His older cousin Baljeet, doing sums on the charpai, looked up. "You've swept that part three times."

Lokesh pretended not to hear. Each job made the tight feeling in his tummy go away for a little while.

Next evening, the tight feeling came back the moment he saw the bag. This time he didn't even open it. He went straight to the calves.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do right after giving the calves fresh water?
qa.a: He wiped his little wooden shelf until it shone.

qa.q: Why does sweeping the courtyard feel sensible to Lokesh, even though nobody asked him to?
qa.a: Each job makes the tight feeling in his tummy go away for a little while. The relief is real, so the chores feel like a good idea even though the exercise is still waiting.

qa.q: What small step could help Lokesh break the pattern?
qa.a: Open the bag and try just the first sentence before any chores, maybe with Baljeet on the charpai beside him. Finding out the first one is doable is a better relief than escaping.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Lokesh's evening?
qa.a: Baljeet notices the courtyard swept three times and can probably tell Lokesh is dodging something. Baljeet may be amused, or a bit worried, and could offer to sit together over the first question.

grounding: A boy avoids his hardest subject by doing chores and asking for water, and the next evening the urge to escape comes even faster.

Emeka, eleven, got home in Toronto at four with a worksheet of French verbs. French was the hardest thing he did all week. He didn't know any of the endings.

He put the worksheet on his desk, face down. Then he wiped the desk with a sock. He sorted his football cards by team. "Mum, can I have some water?" He drank it slowly. "Mum, can I have more water?"

At six his friend Wei texted: "done french?? 😩"

"doing it tomorrow," Emeka typed, and felt light and free for the rest of the evening.

Tomorrow came. When Emeka walked into his room and saw the worksheet still face down, his chest went tight at once. He turned around and went to ask for water before he'd even taken off his shoes.

qa.q: How did Emeka place the worksheet on his desk?
qa.a: He put it face down.

qa.q: Why did Emeka feel light and free after typing "doing it tomorrow"?
qa.a: Pushing the worksheet off to tomorrow took away the scary not-knowing for now, so the relief felt real. It seemed like a fair deal at that moment.

qa.q: What could help Emeka the next afternoon, when his chest goes tight?
qa.a: He could turn the worksheet over and do just one verb, maybe checking with Wei after. Facing a small piece shows him the not-knowing can be handled, instead of feeding the urge to run.

qa.q: What would change if Wei suggested they do the first few verbs together on a call?
qa.a: Emeka might feel less alone with the not-knowing and get started before the dread grew. Wei would probably find it easier too.

grounding: A boy escapes the discomfort of hard French homework with small jobs and water, and the next day the wish to avoid it hits even harder.
